title: File:Neptune and Triton - Voyager 2 (43406970055).png
author: Justin Cowart
description:
Voyager 2's view of Neptune and Triton at around 1640 UT on August 25, 1989. This simulated view combines a wide-angle camera observation of Neptune and a narrow-angle camera observation of Triton taken within half an hour of one another. I then aligned these images using Neptune Viewer to determine the relative positions of the two bodies. Regions of missing data (the right 1/3 of Neptune, the right crescent tip of Triton) were repaired with images acquired after these observations where available.
The position of Voyager 2 with regards to the Neptune system causes a couple of interesting observing effects. First, the crescents are misaligned - the horns of Triton's crescent point in a slightly different direction than Neptune's, due to their positions relative to the Sun from Voyager 2's viewpoint. Additionally, Triton appears about twice as large relative to Neptune than it actually is. This is because Neptune was ~40% further away from Voyager when this image set was taken.

Image Credit: NASA / JPL / Voyager-ISS / Justin Cowart

title: File:Neptune, Moons and Eclipses - Voyager 2 (32895381568).png
author: Justin Cowart
description:
Natural color composite of Neptune imaged by Voyager 2 at 0415UT on August 24, 1989. This composite was taken approximately 24 hours before the spacecraft's closest approach. Three moons, Despina, Galatea, and Larissa are visible. Despina's shadow falls on the planet, creating a short-duration solar eclipse for parts of Neptune's mid-northern latitudes. 
This composite uses orange, green, violet and blue filter images for color. The moons visible here were pulled from various frames and aligned on their locations at 0415UT. The moons, near Voyager's sensitivity limit with this exposure setting, have been brightened by roughly 10x for visibility. Two other moons, Thalassa and Naiad, were theoretically also visible within the raw data, but well below detection limits.

Image Credit: NASA / JPL / Voyager-ISS / Justin Cowart
